Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered for future wireless applications and have been evaluated for their ability to support a wide range of users with varying capabilities. In these systems, it has been observed that certain spatial configurations lead to non-overlapping visibility regions among users, thereby limiting the overall number of possible slots. Specifically, in a recent study involving a 16x16 MIMO system, it was found that all users' visibility areas do not intersect, contradicting the claimed ability of these systems to support an exponentially large number of users. Contrary to the prevailing thought, the underlying reason for this phenomenon is not attributed to the lack of channel knowledge or the use of random slot assignment, but rather to the restricted spatial arrangements. In the SAA protocol, the biggest obstacle to achieving optimal performance and maximizing the number of active users is found to lie in the largest user's visibility area overlapping with the second-largest user's area. Similarly, in the FSA protocol, the main issue arises when the largest user's area stops intersecting with the third-largest user's area. Consequently, in a 16x16 MIMO system, the FSA and SAA protocols are only capable of supporting up to 16 and 15 time slots respectively, falling short of the theoretically calculated maximum of 256. These findings suggest that current research focusing on MIMO systems' capacity for supporting a large number of users is based on inaccurate assumptions. As a result, a re-evaluation of these findings is necessary to aid in the development of more efficient scheduling strategies for these systems. Moreover, researchers are encouraged to explore alternative approaches, such as employing different geometric configurations or alloting slots based on priority levels. Ultimately, further study is required to fully understand the limitations and capabilities of large-scale MIMO systems when it comes to supporting a large number of users with varying capabilities. Furthermore, additional research is necessary to investigate the optimal spacing requirements for these systems in practical scenarios. Lastly, theoretical models requiring non-overlapping visibility areas could be re-examined to use more plausible assumptions.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of an advanced ballot tabulation system called Informed Optical Symbol Recognition for Elections, which utilizes artificial intelligence to instantly translate scanned ballot images into machine-readable format. This research aims to evaluate the system's performance in the same manner as a standard hand-counted audit, which involves verifying a sample of ballots to ensure the tabulation accuracy. Due to its highly automated nature, the conventional audit procedure for this system involves re-scanning selected ballots to ensure the AI-driven recognition was accurate. However, our proposed alternative, Informed OCR Audit, involves manually inspecting the original scanned images to verify the AI's decisions, thus eliminating the need for re-scanning. We contend that this more efficient approach is just as reliable and effective in confirming the system's tabulation accuracy. Our findings, based on two separate election studies in Ohio, demonstrate the Informed OCR Audit's effectiveness and efficiency compared to the conventional method. As a result, we are making a case for incorporating this more efficient audit procedure into the overall system, which we believe will contribute to its legitimacy and trustworthiness. Furthermore, our research suggests that this type of advanced ballot tabulation system, coupled with an Informed OCR Audit, could serve as a model for other electoral systems looking to utilize similar technology. The underlying idea of using an expert review of the original scanned images to validate the AI's recognition, rather than re-scanning the images, is also applicable to various other automated symbol recognition contexts, such as check depositing and document scanning. Therefore, we are confident that our findings will be valuable to these other areas of research. The results of our studies are also available for use by the scientific community.
